title: SEC Logo Quiz: Hard Mode
headline: Can You Name The SEC School From A Tiny Piece Of Its Logo?
description: A hard SEC logo quiz: eight tiny pieces of SEC school logos, about 2% of each logo. Guess the school, tap to reveal the answer, keep score and share your result.
intro: Every piece below is a small square cut from a current SEC school logo, about one fiftieth of the whole mark. No full letters, no team names, no giveaways. Each piece still holds one real detail, a color pair, a curve or an edge that belongs to only one school.
Make your guess, then tap Show The Answer. Be honest and mark whether you got it, and your score adds up at the bottom.

items.piece: A royal blue corner with a white inline, at the bottom of the K.
items.fact: Kentucky's UK monogram is part of the identity it unveiled with Nike in February 2016.

items.piece: Navy and the orange outline along the bottom curve of the U.
items.fact: In 2019 Auburn tightened the space between the A and the U of its interlocking logo.

items.piece: Crimson with a thin white gap, where the O and U overlap.
items.fact: Oklahoma has worn the interlocking OU on a crimson helmet since the 1966 season. Before that the Sooners wore white helmets.

items.piece: The orange, white and blue stripes above the gator's green head.
items.fact: Florida first painted the Gator head at midfield of its stadium in 2012, replacing the F.

items.piece: The curve under the left arm of the orange T.
items.fact: The T first went on Tennessee helmets in 1964, when coach Doug Dickey swapped the numbers on the helmets for it.

items.piece: A front leg of the running hog, cardinal with a black outline.
items.fact: The running hog traces back to the first Running Razorback, drawn by student artist Hank Hancock in 1924.

items.piece: Purple with a gold outline, at the top of the S.
items.fact: LSU's purple and gold go back to 1893, when coach Charles Coates bought purple and gold Mardi Gras ribbon for a football game.

items.piece: The left end of the crossbar in the crimson script A.
items.fact: Alabama's brand rules say the script A may start a word but may never sit in the middle or at the end of one.
